notes.meaning: Ahaz began to rule over Judah during the seventeenth year of King Pekah's reign in the northern kingdom of Israel. This took place around 735 BC, at a time when neighboring nations were threatening Judah with war. Even though Ahaz grew up under a godly father, King Jotham, he chose a completely different path.

Ahaz was twenty years old when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. King David was the model of faithfulness for Judah's rulers, but Ahaz refused to follow David's godly example. A godly family heritage cannot guarantee that a person will choose to trust and obey God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several ancient translations read that Ahaz was twenty-five years old when he took the throne, which avoids the awkward problem of him having a son at only ten or eleven years old.

notes.meaning: Ahaz copied the sinful practices of the kings of northern Israel and the pagan nations God had driven out of Canaan. In his desperation, he even sacrificed his own son by fire, offering the child to false gods like Molech. This terrible act directly violated God's law and brought horrific idolatry into Judah's royal court.

Ahaz offered sacrifices and burned incense at hilltop shrines and under large shade trees all across Judah. Earlier kings had failed to take down these worship places, but Ahaz was the first king of Judah to take part in them himself. By his own actions, he led the entire nation away from the Lord's temple in Jerusalem.

King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah of Israel joined together to attack Jerusalem. Their goal was to remove Ahaz and put a ruler of their own choice on Judah's throne. They surrounded the city, but God protected Jerusalem and would not let them conquer it.

During this war, King Rezin captured the important Red Sea port city of Elath and drove out the people of Judah. The Edomites then took over the city and continued to live there. Losing this port was a heavy blow that hurt Judah's trade and national wealth.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars and ancient translations suggest the text originally meant Edom rather than Aram, meaning Rezin helped the Edomites regain control of Elath from Judah.

notes.meaning: Instead of turning to God for help, Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser, the powerful emperor of Assyria. Ahaz called himself the emperor's servant and son, willingly giving up Judah's independence to become an Assyrian subject. He ignored God's prophets and put his trust in human power instead.

Ahaz took the silver and gold stored in the Lord's temple and his own palace treasuries to pay the king of Assyria. He stripped the sacred wealth dedicated to God to buy military protection from a pagan kingdom. Turning away from God often forces people to give up what is most precious.

The king of Assyria answered the call by marching against Damascus, the capital of Aram, and capturing it. He executed King Rezin and marched the Aramean people away as captives to Kir, fulfilling what the prophet Amos had said would happen. While this broke the siege against Ahaz, it left Judah under the heavy control of Assyria.

Ahaz traveled to Damascus to pay his respects and submit to the king of Assyria. While he was there, Ahaz noticed a pagan altar and was so impressed by its design that he sent detailed plans to Uriah the priest back in Jerusalem. Rather than honoring God's design for worship, Ahaz wanted to copy a foreign shrine.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historians suggest the altar Ahaz saw was an Assyrian military altar, and that he made a copy to honor his new Assyrian master.

notes.meaning: Uriah the priest followed the king's instructions and finished building the new altar before Ahaz returned home. Instead of standing up for God's law, the priest quickly gave in to please the king. This showed that even the spiritual leaders in Jerusalem were compromising the truth.

When Ahaz returned to Jerusalem and saw the completed altar, he stepped forward to offer sacrifices on it himself. By doing this, he took over duties that God had set aside only for ordained priests. His actions showed a bold contempt for the Lord's commands.

Ahaz offered burnt offerings, grain offerings, drink offerings, and blood on his new Damascus-style altar. He carried out the forms of Israel's traditional worship, but he did so on an altar modeled after pagan idols. Using religious rituals while rejecting God's word turns worship into an empty shell.

The original bronze altar made by Solomon had stood right in front of the temple entrance. Ahaz moved it out of its place of honor and pushed it to the north side so his new altar could take its place. By setting God's altar aside, Ahaz showed open disrespect for the Lord's true worship.

Ahaz commanded Uriah to use the new altar for all the daily public offerings of the nation and the personal sacrifices of the king and people. He kept the old bronze altar only for his own private use to seek guidance, likely through pagan divination. He completely pushed God's true altar out of regular public worship.

Uriah the priest obeyed every order King Ahaz gave him without protest. He chose to obey an earthly ruler instead of guarding the holy things of God. When spiritual leaders fear men more than God, the whole community is harmed.

Ahaz cut the side panels off the bronze movable stands, removed their basins, and took the great bronze washing pool off its bronze oxen to place it on a stone floor. He took this valuable bronze either to satisfy the endless tribute demanded by Assyria or for his own projects. In doing so, he stripped Solomon's temple of its beautiful holy furnishings.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some commentators suggest Ahaz damaged these ornate furnishings out of sheer financial necessity, driven to strip the temple bronze to meet repeated Assyrian demands.

notes.meaning: Ahaz removed the covered shelter used on the Sabbath and closed the royal walkway leading from his palace to the temple. He did this out of fear and deference to the king of Assyria, showing how completely he submitted to his foreign overlord. By shutting down these pathways, he symbolically cut off the throne of Judah from the house of God.

The other events of Ahaz's reign were recorded in the official royal histories of Judah's kings. Other scriptures show that he eventually shut the temple doors entirely and spread idolatry across the whole country. His reign brought deep spiritual darkness upon the people.

Ahaz died at only thirty-six years old and was buried in the City of David, though not in the tombs of the kings because of his wicked life. His godly son Hezekiah became king in his place. Hezekiah would soon undo his father's wicked changes and reopen the house of the Lord.
